q: Mountains along the western edge of the region lose height toward the north. What follows for the vineyards at that end?
opts: They are drier and warmer, since the peaks funnel sun onto them
They are cut off from western weather altogether
They ripen roughly a month earlier
exp: The highest summits shelter the southern vineyards most effectively. The lower northern hills leave the rain shadow weaker, which is why the north of the region is the cooler and damper half.

q: Two departments split the vineyard between them, one to the north and one to the south. Which pair?
exp: Bas-Rhin lies north around Strasbourg and Barr, Haut-Rhin south around Colmar. The names follow the river rather than the map: upstream is haut, so the southern half is the high one.

q: Vines are planted from roughly 175 metres up to about 420 metres and no higher. What stops them going further up the hill?
opts: Forest, cold and a season too short to ripen fruit
A legal ceiling written into the appellation
A complete absence of sunshine on the upper slopes
Soils that turn to heavy clay above the treeline
exp: Above the vineyard line the Vosges are wooded and cold, and the growing season runs out before the grapes are ripe. The sweet spot is the lower slope, warm enough to ripen and steep enough to drain.

q: A bone-dry white with piercing acidity, lime and green apple, and a kerosene note creeping in with age, is poured from a tall green flute. Which variety?
exp: Alsace ferments Riesling dry far more often than Germany does, so the acidity stands unbuffered by sugar. The petrol note comes from a compound that builds slowly in bottle and is a sign of maturity rather than a fault.

q: Choucroute garnie arrives at the table, salty and rich with pork and sausage over sharp fermented cabbage. Which Alsace wine is the traditional partner?
opts: A Pinot Gris Selection de Grains Nobles
exp: Acidity is what handles fat and salt, and a dry wine meets the lactic sharpness of the fermented cabbage instead of fighting it. Sweetness alongside that dish reads as cloying within two mouthfuls.

q: A guest asks how an Alsace Riesling will differ from a Mosel Kabinett at a similar price. What is the most reliable answer?
opts: It will be fermented dry and carry more alcohol
It will have been raised in new oak barrels
It will be sweeter and lower in alcohol
It will be a blend of several white varieties
exp: The rain shadow ripens fruit more fully, and the house style is dry, so the wine usually lands between 12.5 and 13.5 percent with no sugar left. A Kabinett is picked lighter and often keeps some.

q: Steel tanks and large old oak foudres are the norm in the region's cellars, and new barriques are rare. What is the reasoning?
opts: Oak of any kind is forbidden by the appellation rules
The wines are bottled too young to spend time in barrel
New oak would bury the aromatics and the sense of site
Barrels cannot be sourced anywhere in the region
exp: A foudre is old, large and effectively neutral, so it lets a wine breathe without flavouring it. Alsace is built on varietal and vineyard transparency, and vanilla and toast obscure both.

q: Two distinct grapes are bottled under one varietal name here, the older small-berried one and a nineteenth-century crossing that ripens earlier. Which name covers both?
exp: Muscat Blanc a Petits Grains is the finer and more perfumed of the two; Muscat Ottonel ripens earlier and copes better with cool sites. Most bottles are a blend of the pair.

q: The first asparagus of spring is served with ham and hollandaise, a dish that defeats most wines. Which Alsace bottle is the traditional answer?
opts: A Gewurztraminer Selection de Grains Nobles
exp: Muscat smells emphatically of grapes yet finishes dry, and that combination of perfume without sugar sits with asparagus where a hard, acid-driven wine turns metallic.

q: Elsewhere in southern France this aromatic grape is turned into sweet fortified wine, while Alsace ferments it out completely. Which grape?
exp: The south stops the fermentation with spirit to make a vin doux naturel. Alsace does the opposite and lets the wine go dry, which is why its version tastes of the fresh grape rather than of syrup.

q: Lychee, rose petal and ginger fill the glass, the colour is deep gold, the acidity is low and the alcohol high. Which grape?
exp: The berry is pink-skinned, which gives both the colour and the phenolic grip. Low acidity is why the wine can taste sweet even when it has been fermented dry.

q: The first half of the name Gewurztraminer is a German word. What does it mean?
exp: Gewurz means spiced, and Traminer points back to Tramin in the Italian Tyrol. The Alsace grape is the aromatic pink-berried mutation of that older, plainer variety.

q: A washed-rind cheese from a valley high in the Vosges is pungent enough to flatten almost any wine. Which local bottle is served with it?
exp: Munster takes its name from the valley on the mountain slope, and Gewurztraminer's weight, perfume and touch of sugar are among the few things that can meet it. Cumin seed is traditionally served alongside.

q: Until the 2007 vintage one Alsace variety was sold under a borrowed Hungarian name that the European Union eventually forced off the label. Which variety?
exp: Tokay d'Alsace, later Tokay Pinot Gris, was retired to protect Hungary's Tokaji. The wine has no connection to Furmint or to Hungary, and the name appears to rest on old legend.

q: A broad, smoky white with ripe pear and a mushroomy edge, fuller than Riesling and softer in acid, is poured with foie gras. Which variety?
exp: Pinot Gris carries more body and often a little residual sugar, and that weight is what stands up to a rich terrine. The same profile makes it the regional choice for roast poultry and game birds.

q: Berries that ripen a dull pinkish grey rather than black betray a mutation of a familiar red grape. Which is the parent?
exp: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are one vine in three suits of clothes. The grey berry still carries pigment in its skin, which is why the wine is deeper in colour and weightier than most whites.
